item.title: Week 11 NFL picks against the spread, predictions for every game: Cowboys have been bad, but their season isn't dead yet
item.description: Can Dallas still rally to catch the Giants and win the NFC East?
item.content:encoded:
No matter what happens with the Dallas Cowboys, good or bad, there will be an overreaction.

You'd think, based on the commentary, that the Cowboys are hopelessly finished for this 2027 NFL season. And the criticism of the defense has been fair. That group has been awful all season, and reached a low point in allowing 584 yards and 46 points to the 49ers last week.

But the reality is, the Cowboys aren't finished this season.

The move to demote defensive coordinator Christian Parker and have Mike Pettine call plays is probably a few weeks too late, but at least it happened. Perhaps nobody can save the Cowboys' defense, but maybe it works. Parker was overwhelmed in his first season coordinating a defense. Pettine has good experience in the role.

And, more importantly to the big picture and where Dallas' season might be headed, the Cowboys play in the NFC East.

It's reasonable to think the Cowboys can't rally, no matter how bad their division is. Dallas is a major reason the NFC East has been a laughingstock of the NFL season. But at 4-6, the Cowboys are not out of range from the 5-3-1 Giants. The Giants are nearly a touchdown underdog this week vs. the Jaguars and the Cowboys are favored over the Tennessee Titans by 7.5 points. If the favorites win in those games, the Cowboys are back in it. Then, Dallas gets the depleted Eagles on Thanksgiving. It's not too much to ask for them to be back to .500 heading into December. DVOA has Dallas with a 32.1% chance to make the playoffs.

So it's not impossible for the Cowboys to make the playoffs, which would be preposterous based on how bad their defense has been, but the division hasn't run away from them. Still, laying 7.5 points to the Titans might be too much. Cam Ward might be turning a corner; he has played well the past two weeks with the Titans giving him more control over the offense at the line of scrimmage. At the very least, Pettine is unlikely to completely fix Dallas' defense in one week. The Titans have been competitive lately, and that's why Tennessee +7.5 is the pick. But even with a close win over the 1-8 Titans, Dallas really will feel like it is alive again this season. And there will be an overreaction to that, as usual.

Here are the rest of the picks against the spread for Week 11 of the NFL season:

Buccaneers (+7) over Lions

Oddsmakers are still confident in the Lions. Detroit has heavy -525 odds to make the playoffs. That makes some sense because the Lions are 7-2 and a very good offensive team. But can the defense get by without defensive end Aidan Hutchinson and linebacker Jack Campbell? It wasn't a good defense before those injuries (though it has been better since safety Brian Branch returned). It's worth testing Detroit by taking a Buccaneers team that was on a bye last week while the Lions were in Germany.

Cardinals (+15.5) over Chiefs

We've reached the point in the season where some of the worst teams are not competitive. Five of the 13 games this week have double-digit spreads, with the two largest spreads of the season. This is one of them. Whenever you take a double-digit underdog in the NFL, it seems like a horrible idea (see: Colts on Thursday). Who wants to spend an afternoon backing Carson Beck at Arrowhead Stadium? But oddsmakers know this and you're not getting any value on the Chiefs. So, if you're in the practice of picking every NFL game against the spread, suck it up and back those big underdogs.

Dolphins (+16.5) over Bills

And here's the biggest spread of the season to date. The Dolphins do fight hard and Kyle McCord looked reasonable last week. Again, fading Josh Allen with a 1-8 team is not pleasant, but point spreads exist for a reason.

Panthers (-2.5) over Ravens

The Ravens are theoretically desperate, but weren't they desperate in Week 10 and the few weeks before that? Maybe Baltimore just isn't good. Jacoby Brissett brings a level of competence to the offense but it wasn't even good enough to beat the winless Chargers on Monday night. The Panthers aren't great either, but they're better than this version of the Ravens.

Bears (-10.5) over Saints

This is not a great week for NFL matchups. Some of these huge spreads will lead to blowouts. This seems like a good candidate. The Bears are coming off a bye and we know they can put up points in a hurry. Meanwhile, there's no real evidence the Saints are any good on either side of the ball (27th in offensive DVOA, 29th in defensive DVOA).

Steelers (-4.5) over Eagles

Always beware a good team that is coming off being embarrassed. We can argue how good the Steelers really are, but they're 6-3 and practically a playoff lock. And there's no question they were embarrassed at Cincinnati. The Eagles have failed to cover in eight of nine games this season and while that's not necessarily predictive, we all have seen the 2026 Eagles play.

Jets (+3) over Chargers

What were we just saying about this week's matchups? These teams have combined for three wins, and one of them came way back in Week 1 by the Jets. The Jets are coming off two straight blowout losses but those were against the Chiefs and Bills. The Chargers aren't really back just because they finally won a game. In a weird way, it could be a letdown spot after winning their first game. Either way, please don't spend time watching this game.

Jaguars (-6) over Giants

The Jaguars are pretty good at blowing out bad teams. In five of their nine games this season they have won by 17 or more points. And this week they get a boost from trade acquisitions Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates III making their Jacksonville debuts. Perhaps it's unfair to list the Giants as a bad team, but they're certainly on a different tier than the Jaguars.

Raiders (+10) over Broncos

We know the deal with the Broncos. They play close games, and find a way to win them. Over their last 20 games, including the postseason, Denver has two double-digit wins: over the Chargers when Los Angeles sat everyone in Week 18 last season, and against the Cardinals in Week 7. This is a tough matchup for Fernando Mendoza, but Las Vegas should be able to keep it within 10 points. Everyone else does against the Broncos.

Vikings (+3) over 49ers

Behold, the one marquee matchup of Week 11! It's a really fun one. Kyle Shanahan's surgical offense vs. Brian Flores' blitz circus is fascinating. There is a pretty short list of reliable Super Bowl contenders and both of these teams should be on it, after we saw Kirk Cousins provide some stability to Minnesota's offense. Nobody has solved the Vikings' defense yet this season. The Packers moved the ball the best of any Vikings opponents back in Week 1, but we saw how the rematch went last week. Minnesota's defense is so good it held the Bears to three points back in Week 2 (Caleb Williams wasn't hurt in that game until midway through the fourth quarter). Let's take the points and see if Shanahan has the answer to Flores' defense.

Commanders (+6.5) over Bengals

Joe Burrow is the hottest quarterback in the NFL and on his way to an MVP. Every time out he seems like a threat to have a 500-yard game. In other words, it's scary to fade him right now. But the Commanders are coming off some extra rest, they should feel reborn a bit by beating the Giants to stay somewhat alive in the NFC East race, and Jayden Daniels is still capable of keeping Washington in the game.

This week: 0-1

Last week: 5-9

Season to date: 68-81-2

item.title: Week 11 Fantasy Football Matchups to Exploit: 5 players you should have in your lineup
item.description: Ray Garvin highlights 5 players you should definitely have in your fantasy football lineups for Week 11.
item.content:encoded:
Cam Ward gets Dallas, Omarion Hampton gets the Jets and Jonah Coleman has earned the workload to take advantage of Las Vegas. Here, Yahoo analyst Ray Garvin goes over five players who have matchups you can exploit for fantasy football in Week 11.

Cam Ward, QB, Titans at Cowboys

If you've been piecing it together at quarterback, this is the week I'd give Ward a shot. He threw for 304 yards and two touchdowns at Cincinnati, went on bye, then came back to complete 28-of-39 passes for 231 yards and two more scores against Jacksonville. Add 80 rushing yards across those two starts and you can see why the fantasy case is getting stronger.

Tennessee has given Ward more control at the line of scrimmage, and he used play-action on a season-high 35.7% of his dropbacks against Jacksonville. He put together both games without Carnell Tate, who returned to limited practice Wednesday. With Wan'Dale Robinson out for the season, there's room for Tate to command more of the passing game if he's back. I'm not counting on him to take over Robinson's exact role, but getting Ward another receiver he trusts would help.

The rushing is the difference between taking a chance on Ward and settling for a quarterback who needs everything to go right through the air. Those 80 yards are worth eight fantasy points on its own. Even if Tennessee has to settle for a field goal, a scramble or two can make that drive count for your lineup.

Then there's Dallas. The Cowboys are last in total defense at 393.8 yards allowed per game, 26th against the pass and last against the run. They just gave up 46 points and three touchdown passes to Brock Purdy. Dallas can put up points on Tennessee, too, which could keep Ward throwing into the fourth quarter. That's the kind of matchup where I'll stream him even if Tate needs another week.

Omarion Hampton, RB, Chargers vs. Jets

Nine carries. Then 13. Then 22. The Chargers finally leaned on Hampton against Baltimore last week, and he gave them 105 rushing yards and a touchdown. He took 22 of the 27 running back carries. Keaton Mitchell had three. Kimani Vidal had two.

We've seen what happens when Hampton gets that kind of work. In his only two games with 20-plus carries, he handled about 82% of the Chargers' running back carries both times. He went for 115 scrimmage yards against Las Vegas and 105 against Baltimore, scoring in both. The receiving work hasn't been consistent enough to bail him out on lighter days, which is why the carry split matters so much.

There's a difference between leading a committee and getting enough work to control your fantasy day. Against Houston, Hampton averaged 4.6 yards per carry and still finished with just 60 yards because he got 13 attempts and didn't catch a pass. Baltimore was his first game with 20 carries since Week 2.

The Jets are fifth in passing yards allowed per game and 30th against the run. They're giving up 135.3 rushing yards per game and have allowed 13 scores on the ground. If I'm the Chargers, I'm leaning on Hampton again. If he's on my fantasy roster, he's in as an RB2.

Luther Burden III, WR, Bears vs. Saints

Rome Odunze, Colston Loveland and Luther Burden III are all in play this week. We saw all three get there against Tampa Bay: Odunze went for 60 yards and a touchdown, Loveland put up 54 yards on four catches and Burden led the group with seven catches for 97 yards and a score. Burden is the one I want to talk about this week.

Over four games before the bye, Burden earned 30 targets on 95 routes and caught 26 passes for 378 yards and three touchdowns. He averaged 94.5 receiving yards in that stretch, and 244 of his yards came after the catch. That's what I want against a Saints defense that plays zone on 81% of its coverage snaps. Chicago can get him the ball underneath and make New Orleans tackle him in space.

The four-game run also includes two different ways for Burden to get there. Against New England, four catches were enough for 130 yards. Against Seattle, he caught seven passes even though his longest gain was 23 yards. If New Orleans keeps him in front of the coverage, the Seattle game shows how he can still get there on volume.

Burden cleared concussion protocol, and I'm starting him as a high-end WR2. You don't have to sit Odunze or Loveland to buy into what Burden's doing.

Ryan Flournoy, WR, Cowboys vs. Titans

I wanted to see what Flournoy's role looked like with Pickens back. Pickens went for 145 yards and three touchdowns against San Francisco, and Flournoy still caught 6-of-7 targets for 71 yards and a score. He now has 22 catches for 272 yards and three touchdowns over his past five games.

Look at where the ball went against the 49ers. Lamb, Pickens and Flournoy drew 38 of Dallas' 49 targets. They accounted for 288 of Dak Prescott's 343 passing yards and caught all five of his touchdowns. With Jake Ferguson expected to miss this game, I'm not chasing a replacement tight end, and I'm not looking to the backfield for a receiving play. The three receivers are where I want exposure.

Tennessee is last in passing yards allowed per game and ranks 31st in pressure rate without blitzing. That's why I like this game from both sides. Dallas can score through its receivers, and its defense gives Ward a chance to answer. Flournoy is still the third option, but I'm comfortable flexing him in a game that could keep both quarterbacks throwing.

Jonah Coleman, RB, Broncos vs. Raiders

Coleman's touches climbed from 11 to 15 to 21 over his past three games. J.K. Dobbins went from six to seven to five over the same stretch. That's 47 touches and 261 scrimmage yards for Coleman against 18 touches and 58 yards for Dobbins. The gap widened right up to the bye.

The Carolina game showed why I trust the role. Coleman averaged just 3.4 yards per carry, but he still got 17 carries, caught four passes and scored on the ground. The week before, four catches against Kansas City were worth 63 yards. In half-PPR, I'll take a back who can keep adding points through the air even when the rushing efficiency isn't there.

That Kansas City game is why I'd take Coleman over a similarly-ranked back who only gets early-down work. He cleared 100 scrimmage yards on 11 carries because he stayed involved through the air. If Las Vegas keeps it close and Denver has to throw more than expected, the receiving role gives Coleman a way to stay useful.

Now, he gets a Raiders defense giving up 4.9 yards per carry and 13 rushing touchdowns through 10 games. Las Vegas has also allowed the sixth-most fantasy points per game to running backs. Dobbins can still get his share, but Coleman's carries, catches and touchdowns before the bye all point to a back Denver already trusts in multiple situations. I'm starting him as an RB2 with room to finish higher.

Missed out on a Yahoo Fantasy x BreakingT drop? You can still purchase any of the weekly shirts here!

So, who made the cut for our list? Here are the five shirts — all available for purchase right now — and a quick recap of the subjects' fantasy exploits so far in 2026.

Joe Burrow: Cincy Joe Cool

Although he's earned the nickname Joe Cool, no quarterback in the NFL is more red-hot than Joe Burrow over the past five weeks of the season. During Cincinnati's five-game winning streak, Burrow has 22 total touchdowns (20 passing, two rushing) and the Bengals have scored at least 30 points in all five contests. In addition to his prolific touchdown totals, Burrow is minimizing his misses, completing 254 passes on 340 attempts for a league-leading 74.1 completion percentage. Burrow has been hyped up as an MVP-caliber QB for the better part of a decade now, but 2026 might be the year Burrow finally wins one.

CeeDee Lamb: CD Lamb

No player in the NFL has been targeted more times than CeeDee Lamb so far this season. The clear focal point of a Dallas offense that needs every point it can get, Lamb has parlayed his league-best 121 targets into 77 catches, 976 yards and eight touchdowns — the final number being his highest since 2023. At 27, Lamb has three games this season with more than 150 receiving yards, marking just the second time in his career he's reached that milestone (four in 2023).

Jaxon Smith-Njigba: ECRA

What is ECRA? Emerald City Route Artist, which, in addition to being a nightmare for opposing defenses, is exactly what Jaxon Smith-Njigba is. A year after leading the NFL with 1,793 receiving yards, the reigning Offensive Player of the Year is aiming for a receiving triple crown. JSN leads all pass catchers with 79 receptions, 1,207 yards and 10 touchdowns. Sam Darnold has dealt with a series of injuries this season, but when you have an ECRA in your offensive arsenal, who you have under center is an afterthought.

Kenneth Walker III: Beware of K9

An early favorite for 2026's fantasy MVP, Kenneth Walker has proven that his Super Bowl MVP performance was no fluke and he does, in fact, have that dog in him. Walker has five multi-score games for the Chiefs this season and is on pace for career-highs in virtually every statistical category — assuming he stays healthy. Walker came into the season with a firm second-round ADP in Yahoo leagues, but is looking like a bona fide league-winner and first-round pick next season.

Kirk Cousins & Justin Jefferson: Family Portrait

Did we just become best friends — again? Yes, Kirk Cousins and Justin Jefferson did just that after the Vikings dealt for the veteran quarterback right before the NFL trade deadline earlier this month. Cousins spent the prime of his NFL career in Minnesota, earning three Pro Bowl nods and compiling a 50-37 record during his six seasons. Jefferson, one of the elite wide receivers in the NFL, put together the best year of his career in 2022 (128-1,809-8), with Cousins at the helm of the offense. Unsurprisingly, in their first game back together, Jefferson had a season high 13 targets and nine catches. Look out for this duo to make a late season push for the playoffs, both in real-life and fantasy.

item.title: Inside the Shanahan-Flores Matchup
item.description: With six teams on bye and the NFL overloading Thanksgiving Week with prime cuts, there is only one game in Week 11 featuring two teams with both winning records and a positive DVOA. Fortunately, it’s a doozy. Kyle Shanahan, head…
item.content:encoded: With six teams on bye and the NFL overloading Thanksgiving Week with prime cuts, there is only one game in Week 11 featuring two teams with both winning records and a positive DVOA. Fortunately, it’s a doozy. Kyle Shanahan, head coach of the San Francisco 49ers, is your current betting favorite for Coach of the Year. His 49ers are second in offensive DVOA, though that’s only due to a Simpson’s Paradox. The 49ers have a higher DVOA than the Bengals both passing and rushing, but a lower overall DVOA because they run more than Cincinnati. San Francisco is scoring a touchdown on 82.8% of red zone drives, the highest of any offense in the 21st century. They may be the hardest offense to stop in football. Brian Flores, defensive coordinator of the Minnesota Vikings, is your current prohibitive favorite for Assistant Coach of the Year. The Vikings are only third in defensive DVOA, but that’s brought down a little bit by run defense in games where they’ve had to be on the field for most of the game. Now that Kirk Cousins appears to have elevated the offense to at least professional levels, the Vikings may have fixed their biggest defensive flaw. Minnesota is allowing a touchdown on only 25.0% of red zone drives, the lowest of any defense in the 21st century. They may be the hardest defense to crack in football. “He’s more unique than all the other 31 guys,” Shanahan said about Flores. “Everything is high level,” Flores said about Shanahan. If you’re going to have one game that matters in a week, it’s good to have arguably the strongest schematic minds in the game going head-to-head in a nationally televised game. The stakes are high, too. Either the 49ers or Vikings have been in first place in the NFC standings every single week this season. That’s not quite guaranteed after Sunday – the Lions would slip into first if both they and Minnesota won – but it’s hard to shake the feeling that this game could well be for the bye week. The 49ers earn the No. 1 seed in 81% of our simulations with a win but only 26% with a loss. The Vikings, in the tougher division, get the No. 1 seed 51% of the time with a win and only 5% with a loss – and those numbers might be soft, because while we’ve adjusted Minnesota’s DAVE to account for having Cousins at quarterback, beating San Francisco would be a good sign that the offense is even better than we thought it could be. A matchup of this caliber deserves the Stats iQ breakdown. And, with all due respect to Cousins, Justin Jefferson, Fred Warner, Nick Bosa et. al., we’ve got to focus on the highlight matchup this week. There’s a stat floating around that Flores is 5-0 against Shanahan in his career. That is correct, but also a little misleading. Flores was a linebacker coach when Shanahan’s Falcons lost in Super Bowl LI, and a defensive assistant when New England beat Shanahan and Washington in 2011. I’m not going to say that Flores didn’t coach up Rob Ninkovich or Jerod Mayo, but I would be hard-pressed to say he was the defining factor of those Patriots defenses. Flores’ 2020 win with the Dolphins over the 49ers is a little more relevant, but that was against a highly injured 49ers team. Sorry, I mean a highly injured 49ers team by 49ers standards. That was the game where Jimmy Garoppolo rushed back into action two weeks after a high ankle sprain and then was sat down at halftime because he clearly and visibly was not right. Flores did have something to do with that, with his defense picking up three sacks and four quarterback hits on Garoppolo in a half, but if anything, the lesson there is to not throw chum to Flores’ sharks. That leaves us with the 2023 and 2024 matchups, both one-score victories for the Vikings. Stats iQ goes all the way back to 2023, so we can use it to look at how Flores played the 49ers both times, and how they responded. In 2023, the Vikings blitzed the 49ers a mere 33.3% of the time, getting pressure on 21.2% of dropbacks and quick pressures on 14.3% of their pressures. All three numbers were significantly lower than their season averages of 51.9%, 28.0% and 40.2%, respectively, but it worked out. While Brock Purdy’s 9.1 yards per attempt and 63.6% success rate were more than any other quarterback against the Vikings that season, he threw two late interceptions on consecutivefourth-quarter drives, Cam Bynum picking his pocket twice. Flores’ strategy was similar in the 2024 game – a 34.9% blitz rate, only with pressure ticking up to 30.8% because the Vikings’ defense was better and the 49ers’ offensive line was worse. Purdy had the second-highest DVOA for a quarterback against that 2024 defense at 24.8%, throwing for 319 yards at an 8.9 yard per attempt clip, but yards per attempt are not yards per dropback. The Vikings sacked Purdy six times, leaving San Francisco in long down-and-distances over and over and adding another interception late in the game for good measure. That’s been the story of Flores versus Shanahan so far. He dials back the blitzes, accepting a lower pressure rate, and still finds success. The 49ers are a dangerous team to blitz, because they are so good at finding those hot routes and the gaps in the middle of the defense left behind by those blitzing defenders: George Kittle or Christian McCaffrey slipping into the holes voided by missing linebackers and Purdy hitting them. So far this season, no quarterback has been better against the blitz than Purdy, his 334 DYAR and his 49.0% DVOA. He’s even third in the league with 85 rushing DYAR on his scrambles. Add in the thinner air in Mexico City possibly requiring more defensive substitutions, and it seems almost certain that the Vikings will blitz less on Sunday night than they have all season. But what does “blitz less” even mean in connection to the 2026 Vikings? They currently are blitzing 71.8% of the time and haven’t had a game yet where they’ve blitzed less than 57.7% of the time. The Vikings are first in ESPN’s pass rush win rate, so they’re winning all their individual battles, but their pressure rate drops to 32.9% when they don’t send someone from out of position. That being said, “non-blitzed dropbacks” is such a small sample size – we’re talking just 87 dropbacks this season. And they still have five interceptions and nine sacks when not blitzing – a rate of 16.1%, compared to “just” 14.9% when blitzing. It turns out that while Minnesota’s philosophy is based around blitzing like crazy and causing chaos, they’re actually just pretty darn good in general. They’ve also shown little fear of blitzing, even against other quarterbacks who are good at it. Take out the Vikings game, and Jared Goff is the second-best quarterback in the league against the blitz. Remember, we wrote a whole article about that in the leadup to the Lions-Vikings game? But his DVOA drops from 41.9% to 31.3% when you add the Vikings game back in; Minnesota blitzed him 29 times. Goff didn’t completely wilt under pressure; his 5.8% DVOA against Flores is the second best for a quarterback against the Vikings’ blitz so far this season. Unlike Goff, Purdy has succeeded both against the blitz and pressure in general, so I do still suspect Flores will treat him a little more gingerly – a lot more simulated pressures than normal. Two of Purdy’s three picks against Flores’ defense came with some sort of sim pressure; while Purdy has improved over the last two years, it’d be criminal not to try that again. The 49ers, meanwhile, are first in pass block win rate, though they had some issues against Dallas last week. Our charting had right guard Connor Colby allowing five pressures against Dallas, right tackle Colton McKivitz with three and all-everything tackle Trent Williams with four. Half of Williams’ pressures weren’t quick, and you can forgive him a little for eventually giving in when Purdy held the ball for a while, but that’s still a ton of pressure given up against a not particularly threatening defense. 48% of those three players’ pressures allowed happened last week! If that wasn’t a one-game fluke, the 49ers could be in serious trouble. The 49ers’ pass DVOA has been lower the last few weeks than it started the season, but that should be helped by the return of Mike Evans, who got in his first practice in a month on Thursday and looks good to go for Sunday night. The closest defense to Minnesota that San Francisco has played this season is probably Seattle, and Evans was the difference maker in that game. Evans had four catches for 66 yards and a score in tight coverage against the Seahawks, and the ability to just throw the ball up and assume that Evans is going to out-fight the defender for it is an incredible safety valve for an offense. 52.5% of Evans’ targets this year have come in tight coverage, the most for any qualified receiver in the league. His 26.9% DVOA in tight coverage is second in the league, and one of only four wideouts to have positive DVOA in tight coverage this season. The Vikings are fourth in the league, with 34.2% of targets against them coming in tight coverage, so Evans being available is a huge boon. We’ll see how much he plays, coming off an Achilles injury and in the thin atmosphere in Mexico City, but any Evans is a good amount of Evans. Evans is just one weapon San Francisco has. And the real test might be whether or not they use all five. If you want to see early on who is dictating the game, watch to see how many players Shanahan deploys on routes. The Vikings have faced five eligible receivers running routes on pass plays just 37.5% of the time. That is by far the lowest in the league; next is the Giants at 58.5%. From a combination of fear and necessity, teams change their entire offense to try to protect themselves from the Flores blitz, backs and tight ends stuck trying to keep quarterbacks upright – and usually futilely. The 49ers, though? They get all five eligibles out on 80.1% of their passing plays – the highest rate in the NFL. That will often include a chip block or two, and you can expect to see a lot of that in this game, with George Kittle and Kyle Juszczyk taking a moment to slow a Dallas Turner or Andrew Van Ginkel down before leaking out into a route. But that’s the way Shanahan attacks the blitz – if you are going to overcommit guys to rushing the passer, that is going to leave the back of your defense thin, and someone, somewhere, is going to win a matchup. That won’t always be Christian McCaffrey on Von Miller-levels, but Shanahan is known for putting linebackers in a blender, finding mismatches and taking advantage of them. The Vikings have very good coverage linebackers and edge rushers – Van Ginkel, in particular, is allowing just a 18.8% success rate when targeted this season, but the 49ers offense is designed in a lab to make mismatches. Can Shanahan continue to send everyone out, getting those mismatches and finding someone to attack before Flores’ pass rush can get home? Or will Flores’ relentless pressure force Shanahan off of his game, forcing him to keep Kittle and CMC and Juszczyk back to try to prevent Purdy from being ground into a fine powder? That’s the easiest single thing to watch to see who is winning this game – not so much whether the plays work or not, but which coach is forced to submit to the other, changing their game plan because the other guy’s is working so well. Can Shanahan stretch Flores’ pass rush to its breaking point? Can the back end of Flores’ defense hold up enough to wreck the timing and scheme of Shanahan’s play designs? Tell me that answer, and I’ll tell you who wins the game. And we haven’t even gotten to the run game yet! One philosophy to beat the Vikings has been to keep pounding the rock at them, wearing them down. The Vikings kind of only have one layer of their defense thanks to all the blitzing; if you can get through the front layer of the defense, there is open space behind them, as linebackers zip in from here, there and everywhere. The Vikings are 10th in adjusted line yards at 4.07, but they fall to 26th in second-level yards and 23rd in open-field yards. Getting past the initial surge of rushers is very difficult, but all that movement and simulated pressure means that there are gaps left open in the running game, and if you can find them, you can find a lot of open space in front of you. That said, while Minnesota ranks 11th in run defense, there’s a pretty severe first/second half split going on there. The Vikings actually have the best run defense in the league in the first two quarters, at -26.2% DVOA. They fall to 26th in the third and fourth quarters at -0.9% DVOA. They assume – they hope! – that the offense will actually be able to stay on the field now with Cousins, but it’s possible the benefits of that will be counteracted by the thin atmosphere. And it’s worth noting that the gap between their adjusted line yards and their second-level and open-field performance is there in the first half as well; it’s just that the unit as a whole has been better in the first half. If you’re looking to attack them, inside zone is the weakness. Even just looking at the first half, when they’re fresh, the Vikings have an -18.7% DVOA against inside zone, 14th in the league. And, again, that’s tipped towards big plays rather than consistent, down-to-down success – they’re only allowing a 30.4% success rate, but 2.39 yards after contact and an 8.7% explosive rate allowed are both in the bottom 10, when they’re still supposed to be fresh and active. Christian McCaffrey has the third-highest DVOA in the league running inside zone, at 27.6%. The 49ers don’t run that much of it, all in all – just 57 attempts this season, or about a half dozen a game – but it’s their counterpunch. They want to stretch you to the outside first and then, when you’re over-pursuing, hit you on the inside. I would expect San Francisco to attack the interior of the Vikings defense earlier and more frequently than usual, trying to catch Flores’ defenders vacating their spots. Which again leads to another reason Flores should blitz less! It’s the best chess game in the league in 2026, and it will be an absolute treat to watch after what looks like a pretty milquetoast Sunday of football. Grab your popcorn, folks; we’re in for a good one.

item.title: Cowboys vs. Titans: Matchups to watch in Week 11
item.description: These matchups will be the key to a Cowboys win
item.content:encoded:
This Week 11 matchup between the Dallas Cowboys (4-6) and the Tennessee Titans (1-8) is an interesting one. Both teams have struggled this season. The Cowboys are still somehow in playoff contention thanks to a suspect NFC East, while the Titans currently hold the No. 1 overall pick in the 2027 NFL Draft.

The Cowboys are clearly the more talented team, but you wouldn’t know it by the way they’ve continued to disappoint at nearly every turn thus far this season. Because of that you can’t quite count out the Titans pulling off the upset. The best way for the Cowboys to secure another “W” just to win certain matchups, which we’ve listed below.

Cowboys’ defense vs. Titans RB Tony Pollard

Christian McCaffrey absolutely shredded the Cowboys defense last week and you can bet Tony Pollard is hoping to do the same against his former team both on the ground and through the air. He’s currently on a hot streak over the last three games averaging 130 yards from scrimmage and two touchdowns per game. On the ground he’s averaging 93 rushing yards per game and 4.8 yards per carry. Considering the Cowboys are allowing 154.1 rushing yards per game and 5.2 yards per carry, there’s a good chance Pollard’s hot streak continues.

DT Quinnen Williams vs. Titans OL

If there is someone playing better than Quinnen Williams is over the past month or so, it’s by a slim margin. No. 92 has been a one-man wrecking crew on what is arguably the worst defense in the entire league. He’s playing like the All-Pro he is, and is the one bright spot for the Cowboys putrid defense thus far this season. He should once again wreak havoc against the Titans interior offensive line in Week 11. We fully expect him to make some game-changing plays as both the run and pass defender, possibly adding a couple more QB sacks to his total.

Cowboys’ aerial attack vs. Titans secondary

This is one of those strength versus weakness matchups that should heavily favor the Cowboys. Allowing 266.9 passing yards per game, the Titans defense currently ranks dead last in the category. On the flipside, the Cowboys are averaging 265.5 passing yards per game, which currently ranks third overall in the NFL. With CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens both capable of dropping in 100+ yard receiving game at any moment, and with Ryan Flournoy coming up clutch lately, the Dak Prescott led aerial attack should feast this week.

item.title: NFL predictions: 4 keys to a Lions victory over the Buccaneers in Week 11
item.description: Predicting what the Detroit Lions will do to earn a victory over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 11 of the 2026 season.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions (7-2) and Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-6) will face off at Ford Field in Detroit in a Week 11 showdown. The Lions and Bucs have faced each other four times in the last three seasons, and these two teams know each other almost as well as their head coaches.

“Tampa Bay Bucs, competitive, physical unit,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said of the Bucs. “Known (Buccaneers Head Coach) Todd Bowles a long time. Obviously have got a ton of respect for him and what he’s about. And this defense is playing outstanding football. And offensively, they’re committed to the run game, time of possession. They’re trying to force you into making errors. And really, the last three games, they played some pretty good football.”

This week’s prediction preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook, who currently have the Lions listed at +2000 to win this year’s Super Bowl and are currently 6.5-point favorites in Week 11. Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will beat the Bucs in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint.

Bucs base scheme

For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 11 preview: Breaking down the Bucs’ offensive and defensive schemes.

Prediction 1: Lions continue to feed 14

Germany was a storybook celebration of Amon-Ra St. Brown. The Lions All-Pro receiver may have made only four receptions, but he chewed up 98 yards, and both touchdown receptions were epic.

As fantastic as Germany was for St. Brown, it’s not his only source of energy; he has a history of repeating big-game success against specific opponents. For example, St. Brown always shows up big when the Lions play the Bills, but after Buffalo, he’s consistently had the most success against the Buccaneers.

Over four games, St. Brown’s per-game averages include: 9.25 receptions, 101.5 receiving yards, and .75 touchdowns:

  • 2025: 6 receptions, 86 yards, 1 touchdown
  • 2024: 11 receptions, 119 yards
  • 2023 (Playoffs): 8 receptions, 77 yards, 1 TD
  • 2023: 12 receptions, 124 yards, 1 TD

The Bucs run a tight bump-and-run press at the line of scrimmage, and they operate out of zone coverage on nearly 85% of defensive snaps. St. Brown excels at beating press with his precision route running, quickness, and strength, and he’s often quarterback Jared Goff’s first read because the All-Pro receiver is elite at finding soft spots in the zone.

Add in the fact that the Bucs blitz nearly 44% of the time (second most in the NFL), and St. Brown will often set up behind the linebackers, secure catches in volume, and churn out yards after the catch (YAC). This is the fifth time in four years St. Brown has faced this defense, so he should have a strong feel for its weaknesses in zone.

Feed the hot hand.

Prediction 2: Gibbs attacks edges on the ground and through the air

Prediction No. 1 last week was to attack the edges of the Patriots’ defensive line, and it played out to perfection. This week, I am calling for it again, not only because it’s working, but it’s also worked in the past against this defense.

Here’s a look at Gibbs numbers from the last four games against the Bucs, noting that he was injured and inactive in the first meeting, and splitting touches with David Montgomery in the other three games:

  • 2025: 17 rushes, 136 yards (8.0 ypc), 2 TDs — 3 receptions, 82 yards
  • 2024: 13 rushes, 84 yards (6.5 ypc), 0 TDs — 7 receptions, 22 yards
  • 2023 (P): 9 rushes, 74 yards (8.2 ypc), 1 TD — 4 receptions, 40 yards
  • 2023: Inactive

Three things stand out when looking at those statistics: 1) the rushing yards per carry numbers are gaudy; 2) the Lions aren’t afraid to find Gibbs through the air, as it can be highly productive and effective in slowing down the Bucs’ blitz; and 3) if this is what he produced in a part-time role, can he exceed these numbers?

It would be a lofty expectation for Gibbs to maintain this level of success, especially since the Bucs allow only 79.1 rushing yards per game (best in the NFL), 3.5 yards per carry (3rd best), -0.13 EPA on runs against them (3rd), and a 38.3% rushing success rate (4th).

However, if we look back at the last five weeks (four games for the Bucs), Tampa Bay’s run defense numbers have been closer to average than elite: 87 rushing yards per game, 3.87 ypc (10th), -0.05 EPA on runs against (18th), and a 42.2% success rate (19th) allowed.

Over that same time period, the Lions have won five straight games, and Gibbs is averaging 99.2 yards per game (best in the NFL)—eclipsing 100 rushing yards in four of the last five games—, 5.28 yards per carry (5th), -0.02 EPA (9th), and a 43.6% success rate (10th).

The Bucs run defense is formidable, but they’ve been slightly vulnerable lately, and with the odds-on favorite for Offensive Player of the Year honors in your backfield (according to FanDuel Sportsbook), you need to get the ball into his hands.

Prediction 3: Lions load the box to stop the run

The Bucs rushing attack is one of the best in the NFL, and it’s carried the team through some rough patches. Statistically, they rank No. 1 in the NFL in rushing yards per game (163.9), rushing yards per play (5.0), explosive rushing plays over the last four games (16.1%), and 20+ yard runs (11). While some of those stats may be skewed by the “monsoon” game, where the Bucs attempted only three passes and ran the ball 56 times for 324 yards, they’re still in the top 5 in most rushing categories even without that anomaly.

The Bucs deploy a two-headed rushing attack with Bucky Irving and Kenneth Gainwell, but Irving is the starter and Tampa Bay will often ride his hot hand. Here’s Next Gen Stats with more on Irving:

“Bucky Irving enters Week 11 of 2026 with 825 rushing yards, 5th in the NFL, including two games with 150-plus rushing yards (tied for 2nd in the NFL, trailing only Jahmyr Gibbs with four). Irving has recorded seven scrimmage touchdowns since Week 5, tied for 2nd in the NFL behind only McCaffrey (9). His 91.7 rushing yards per game in 2026 would rank as the second-most in a single season in Buccaneers history, trailing only James Wilder’s 96.5 rush yards per game in 1984.”

The Bucs use a blend of blocking schemes, including outside zone, inside zone, and counter, but they lean most on “gap” concepts. According to Next Gen Stats, the Bucs utilize a gap blocking scheme on “29.7% of their designed carries (5th highest rate) and on these runs have recorded a league-leading 415 rushing yards,” with Irving accounting for over half that production (230 yards).

However, as Next Gen also points out, the Lions have done well against gap concepts this season, allowing only 3.3 yards per carry (6th fewest) and just one touchdown this season from this scheme. Overall, the Lions’ run defense has been steady and is improving as the season rolls on. They’re 5th in the NFL in yards allowed per game (90.4), No. 1 in preventing yards after contact, and in their last four games, they’ve allowed a rushing success rate of only 33.8% (3rd best).

This is a real strength-on-strength matchup, according to Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard:

“They’re the number one rush offense in the League and we’re one of the top premier run defenses in the League. […] They don’t hide it, and we don’t hide the way we play. So it’s a beautiful thing. It’s a beautiful challenge, and we’re looking forward to it.”

With the Bucs passing offense struggling (they’re bottom-five in most statistical categories) and the rushing attack being their biggest weapon, look for the Lions to load the box—potentially utilizing three safety sets following the return of Kerby Joseph—and lean on players like Brian Branch to live near the line of scrimmage and try to slow down Irving and the Bucs ‘ run game.

Prediction 4: Lions win turnover battle

The Bucs defense has been very opportunistic this season and currently leads the NFL with 21 forced turnovers (16 interceptions, 5 fumbles recovered) through nine games. They’re +7 overall in turnover ratio (3rd), as the Bucs offense has turned the ball over 14 times (9 interceptions, five fumbles lost).

The defense has been on fire of late. Of their 21 turnovers forced, 13 came in the last three games, including picking off Bears QB Caleb Williams four times in their last outing, and they’ve turned those turnovers into 57 points, the third-highest total in the NFL—that’s over 28% of their total points scored for the season (202).

“Well, they are opportunistic,” Campbell said of the Bucs ‘ ability to generate turnovers. “Obviously (Buccaneers Coach Todd Bowles) he’s always done it. He pressures a lot, throws a lot at you and forces you into errors, […] They’re well coached. The disguises are good. They’ve got a counter look for a look. They want to show you the picture, but now it could be three different coverages and pressures. So, they do a really good job of that, and that’s it. They want to force you into errors.”

Jared Goff’s first six games of the season were clean: no turnovers and 14 touchdowns. But Goff has run into some bad luck (Jameson Williams slipping on a route) and made a few questionable throws, resulting in four interceptions over the last three games. Overall, the Lions have done well in the turnover department this season and are +2 through nine games (13th). But they’ve also fumbled twice in the last month and are -2 net over the last four.

But the Lions offense isn’t alone with their recent struggles in this department: the Bucs offense has been loose with the ball. Baker Mayfield is dealing with a thumb injury in his throwing hand, is coming off a two-interception performance with wildly inconsistent accuracy, and had three fumbles the week prior in their “monsoon” game. Bucky Irving has also fumbled three times in the last three games (one in each), but has been fortunate to only lose one to the opponent.

The comfy confines of Ford Field and home-field advantage have favored the Lions, and in the four games they’ve played in Detroit, they’ve forced six turnovers (including at least one in each game) while giving up just four. Even a minor advantage or break-even scenario should be considered a win for the Lions because turnovers have played a big part in keeping the Bucs in games or letting them slip away, and the Lions won’t want to give them any chances to stick around in this one.

item.title: Week 11 Fantasy Football Start/Sit Advice: What to do with Brock Purdy, Emeka Egbuka, more players
item.description: Scott Pianowski plays traffic cop, offering start/sit lineup advice for some key players in fantasy football Week 11.
item.content:encoded:
Start-sit decisions can be vexing for even the best of fantasy football managers. If you need help setting your fantasy football lineups, Scott Pianowski offers some assistance with his Week 11 traffic report.

Green Light ✅

QB Cam Ward at Cowboys: The Titans have stepped up their pass frequency the last two weeks and Ward has also started to scramble more. And the Cowboys present a dream matchup, fielding perhaps the worst defense in the league. This looks like a pinball game, so give Ward some quarters and stand back.

TE Chig Okonkwo vs. Bengals: The trendy TE sleeper hasn't fully popped yet, still stuck on zero touchdowns. But Okonkwo has 15 targets the last two games and the Bengals have struggled to defend the seam all season. Jayden Daniels trusts Okonkwo, and fantasy managers should as well.

TE Mark Andrews at Panthers: Nobody expected Jacoby Brissett to fully save Baltimore's season, but at least he kept the offense functional in his first start with the Ravens. Brissett is usually good for passing volume and he loves to target his tight ends, so a now-healthy Andrews is back in fantasy relevance.

RB Omarion Hampton vs. Jets: It's been no fun to back the LAC offense this year, but Hampton had a 22-105-1 statement against Baltimore on Monday, and now he faces a New York rushing defense that's been lousy all year. Hampton probably can't pay off his summer ADP, but he might get back into the RB2 area.

Yellow Light 😕

QB Brock Purdy vs. Vikings (Mexico): Purdy has been inside the QB1 cutline in 7-of-9 starts this year, and he's coming off QB4 finishes in back-to-back weeks. The Minnesota defense is a major challenge, but the aggressive Vikings will also give up some chunk plays when the blitzes don't get home. Unless your other option is in a great spot, I'll keep Purdy in my lineup, trusting his decision-making and the creative schemes of Kyle Shanahan.

RB Ollie Gordon II at Bills: Solving for workload is most of the battle when we handicap running backs, and Gordon averages 21 touches over the last five games. The Buffalo rushing defense has also been below average all year. Even if this game gets out of hand, Gordon is still likely to get 15 or more opportunities, keeping him in the RB2 mix.

WR Adonai Mitchell at Chargers: The catch-less game two weeks ago spooked fantasy managers, and Mitchell only secured three of his eight targets last week. But we have to consider that his routes are usually downfield, which means volatility — but big returns when they do click. Mitchell remains in the WR3 lobby during this challenging Week 11, especially with Omar Cooper Jr. ruled out.

WR Jaylen Waddle vs. Raiders: He's still the No. 1 wideout in Denver, though Pat Bryant's return could skim a few targets. With Bo Nix struggling in his third season (6.0 YPA, 84.7 rating), Waddle can't be viewed as an automatic start against anyone.

Red Light 🚨

WR Jalen Coker vs. Ravens: His fun breakout season has fallen apart over the last four weeks, managing just seven catches and 74 yards over that span. The Panthers have also gotten wider with their pass distribution, and the offense runs through Chuba Hubbard anyway. Coker belongs on our benches until a show-me game.

WR Emeka Egbuka at Lions: Normally we start any name-brand player when Detroit comes up on the schedule, but the Buccaneers haven't thrown the ball proactively all year. Baker Mayfield is tracking to start but isn't 100% yet, another reason to be careful with the Tampa Bay passing game.

TE Travis Kelce vs. Cardinals: He hasn't scored a touchdown since Week 3 and the passing game is getting more crowded too, with Emmett Johnson starting to pop and Josh Downs now in the WR room. Kelce should be viewed as TE2 depth option for the rest of the season.

RB Travis Etienne Jr. at Bears: New Orleans is likely to use three backs at Chicago and the game could get out of hand quickly against the high-powered Bears' offense. The Saints have also struggled to run block all season. Etienne isn't a proactive play in this spot.
